newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU seen falling behind in information technology.
newsitem.headline: EU seen falling behind in information technology.

text.p: Europe is falling behind competitors in crucial information and communication technology (ICT) industries, according to a report which will be debated by European Union industry ministers on Saturday.

The study, carried out by consultancy Booz-Allen & Hamilton, calls for "dramatically accelerated" reform to help boost the position of Europe's ICT industries, which are seen as vital for creating future jobs and boosting economic growth.
"Overall, European competitiveness in ICT sectors lags substantially behind the U.S. and/or Japan in all major sectors except public telecommunications equipment," it said.
"A significant factor contributing to Europe's fading competitiveness is the fragmentation of Europe's ICT-related policies, standards and infrastructure elements," it said.
The EU appeared to be stuck in the middle, it said.
"On the one side stagnating in share of traditional mass market products; and on the other side falling behind the U.S. in the critical growth areas of software and content," it said.
The study, commissioned by the Dutch Ministry of Economic Affairs and due to be released on Saturday, compares the EU market with those of the United States, Japan and Korea.

The Netherlands, the current EU president, will host the informal ministerial meeting in The Hague, which is to focus on Europe's industrial competitiveness -- which in general lags behind rival superpowers the United States and Japan.
The ICT sectors in the study represented an EU market of some 300 billion European currency units ($350 billion) in 1995.

The U.S. industry had "outgrown" its counterparts in Europe, Japan and Korea -- especially in software, consumer electronics, information technology hardware and private network equipment, the report said.
One of the major bottlenecks in Europe is a shortage of qualified personnel, it said, with firms lagging 50 percent behind U.S. rivals in the critical area of the value added by each employee.
In emerging software markets that are key for multimedia services, Europe's competitive position is "very weak" with 18 of the 20 top vendors being from the United States.
The European telecoms sector is becoming increasingly competitive as liberalisation proceeds, but varying stages of deregulation are causing a fragmented landscape, it said.

In the highly competitive semiconductor sector, Europe has so far held a relatively stable position, but in information technology hardware and consumer electronics it has experienced a small loss of production share.
To be successful, Europe has to create a truly harmonised market with minimal regulatory impediments, the report said.

It listed a number of possible policy actions to help overcome the problems, including the creation of a regulatory framework covering all ICT sectors, an ICT-related research & development programme, a single European standardisation agency for all concerned sectors and an initative to boost skills.
"ICT policy reform must be accelerated in a way that solicits and leverages industry collaboration," it said.

Offering some hope, the study said the "picture is not unduly grim" if European governments and industry can work together effectively, as they have for example in developing GSM mobile phone networks.

Given that EU unemployment stands at 11 percent, compared with 5.5 percent in the United States and three percent in Japan, "enhanced European competitiveness in ICT could provide a platform to improve employment and create the basis for industrial and societal growth," the study said.
